tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (src/ParserBench.cpp plus src/Bench*.cpp in ArashPartow/math-parser-benchmark-project); the README summary and the committed logs print the compiler (MSVC 1913, 32-bit Release) and CPU (Intel Xeon E5-2687W 0 @ 3.10GHz), and the Release|Win32 flags are in the public math-parser-benchmark-project/math-parser-benchmark-project_msvc2017.vcxproj. First-party (ExprTk's author maintains the suite), but A does not depend on who ran it.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README example summary (bench_expr.txt, 74 expressions, 5,000,000 iterations each): ExprTk (double) 901 points, score 100; muparser 2.2.4 517 points, score 37; FParser 4.5 584 points, score 43; TinyExpr 354 points, score 31; atmsp 1.0.4 530 points, score 38. Per-expression example: ExprTk 39.963 ns versus muparser 2.2.4 47.358 ns on '(a^2/sin(2*pi/b))-a/2' (about 1.18x, derived from page data). Score is the mean over expressions of (ExprTk time / parser time) x 100 per src/ParserBench.cpp, so score 100 versus 37 means muparser runs on average at 37% of ExprTk's per-expression speed, about 2.7x (derived from page data); the README itself only says the reference parser is ExprTk.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: MSVC 1913 (Visual Studio 2017, toolset v141), Release|Win32 (32-bit) per math-parser-benchmark-project_msvc2017.vcxproj: Optimization MaxSpeed (/O2), InlineFunctionExpansion AnySuitable, IntrinsicFunctions, FavorSizeOrSpeed Speed, WholeProgramOptimization, FloatingPointModel Precise, NDEBUG, _SECURE_SCL=0 (flags are not printed in the results log; the vcxproj read is the current HEAD). The repo .pro file builds with g++ -std=c++11 -march=native -fopenmp -O3.
corrections.caveats: The shootout suite is maintained by ExprTk's own author, so it is first-party even though code, compiler, flags and CPU are public. Score is the arithmetic mean of per-expression time ratios against ExprTk (failed rounds count 0), so it is inflated by expressions ExprTk constant-folds or special-cases; single-expression gaps are much smaller (1.18x over muparser on the README example). The README summary is labelled an example and does not match the committed 2018 bench_expr.txt log (logs/shootout_20180421_00.zip, Shootout_20180420_182359.txt: ExprTk 885 points score 100, muparser 2.2.4 523 points score 38, FParser 4.5 score 43). In the same zip's bench_expr_complete.txt run (6617 expressions, 100000 iterations) ExprTk scores 100 versus muparser 2.2.4 score 28, FParser 4.5 32, TinyExpr 15, METL 42. muparserSSE (float, AsmJit JIT) out-scored ExprTk (double) on 5 of the 8 2018 logs (score 110 to 168) and won on points in bench_expr_complete (78987 versus 77945); it ranks lower elsewhere mainly because its float results fail the precision check. Several rival parsers are old versions bundled in the repo ('may contain outdated versions'; muparser 2.2.4 predates the 2.3 series), and the published runs are 32-bit MSVC only. Last-commit date is the year-stamped commit date from the GitHub commit feed (2025-01-01 is how the author dates commits).

notes: Numbers on the README match the record; tier A holds because code, compiler, public vcxproj flags and CPU are all available. Shortcomings to record: first-party suite, score metric is a mean of time ratios inflated by constant-folded expressions (per-expression win over muparser can be only about 1.2x), muparserSSE beats ExprTk on score in most 2018 logs, bundled baselines are old versions, 32-bit MSVC only, repo stale (last commit 2025-01-01).

tier_reason: First-party 2003 report by the FANN author; the benchmark programs are public in its appendix (B.3.3 performance.cc, B.3.4 benchmark.sh at fann.sourceforge.net/report/node12.html) and the CPUs are named, but the compiler and flags are not stated, and it is not peer-reviewed, so it stays C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: AMD Athlon, four layers of 128 neurons: "the fann (thres) library is 238.583 times faster than the jneural library and the fann library is 164.388 times faster than the jneural library"; table: lwnn 4.007 ns per connection (127.074x jneural), jneural 509.138 ns, so standard fann is about 3.10 ns and about 1.29x faster than lwnn (derived from page data). At 512 neurons: fann 64.867x jneural (about 8.07 ns, derived) versus lwnn 8.662 ns and jneural 523.175 ns, so fann is about 1.07x lwnn (derived from page data). At 8 neurons lwnn (11.962 ns) is faster than standard fann per the text. iPAQ, 128 neurons: fann (fix) 188.134 ns per connection versus jneural 13,108.617 ns, "almost 70 times faster than the jneural library and more than 40 times faster than the lwnn library"; the 2.7x remark compares fann (fix) on the iPAQ with jneural on the Athlon. README: "up to 150 times faster execution than other libraries" (no baseline named).
corrections.workload: Execution time per connection (nanoseconds) for fully connected four-layer ANNs with equal layer sizes (doubling from 1 neuron; 128 neurons per layer is the headline case), each size executed continuously for 20 seconds, on an AMD Athlon XP 1600+ (1400 MHz) and on a 206 MHz StrongARM iPAQ H3600 without an FPU, from Steffen Nissen's 2003 FANN report.
corrections.caveats: Author's own 2003 report, measured on 2003 hardware against two obscure libraries (jneural, lwnn); no comparison with any current ML library. The benchmark programs (performance.cc, benchmark.sh) are printed in the report's appendix B.3.3/B.3.4 but are not in the current repo (no benchmarks directory), and the compiler and flags are not named (only 'same compiler and the same compile-options'). Table values come from the LaTeX ALT text of image tables on the page (lwnn 4.007 ns and 127.074x, jneural 509.138 ns at 128 neurons; lwnn 8.662 ns, jneural 523.175 ns at 512). The 238.583x headline uses fann (thres), a threshold activation that does not compute the sigmoid, so it is not the same computation as the baselines; the like-for-like figure is 164.388x for standard fann. Against lwnn the win is small (about 1.3x at 128 neurons, about 1.07x at 512) and lwnn is faster at 8 neurons. The README '150 times' figure names no baseline.

notes: Report page and its image-table ALT text confirm the ratios; the earlier caveat that WebFetch reads disagreed is superseded by the ALT text values. Shortcomings to record: 2003 first-party report on 2003 hardware against obscure jneural/lwnn, compiler and flags unnamed, benchmark code only in the report appendix, 238x headline uses a non-sigmoid activation, only about 1.3x over lwnn and slower than lwnn on small nets.

tier_reason: First-party README table naming CPU (Intel Xeon Skylake @ 2.0 GHz) and compiler (Intel 17.0 x64) but no flags, no libnoise version and no public benchmark code (the preview app is a release binary; the repo holds only the library), and the 68x cellular gap over libnoise exceeds 50x with flags unstated, so C.

corrections.caveats: First-party table from an ICC-built binary on one Skylake Xeon; the benchmark program is a separate preview app in Releases and its code, compiler flags and the libnoise version are not stated. The cellular row against libnoise (68x) is above 50x and likely reflects libnoise's cellular implementation rather than SIMD alone. The scalar FastNoise baseline is the same author's library, and cubic SSE2 (3516) is slower than it (2979); the FastNoise cubic value is identical to the FastNoise cellular value (2979), which may be a copy error in the table. The wiki 'In-depth SIMD level' page compares only SIMD levels within the library, not libnoise. The last commit (2021-03-20, 'Fix noise output error') postdates the table. Repository archived 2 April 2021 and marked deprecated in favour of FastNoise2; AVX-512 numbers need a Skylake-X class CPU.

notes: README table matches the record exactly and the derived ratios check out (Perlin 9.3x/4.2x/1.7x, cellular 68x/45x/20x versus LibNoise). Shortcomings to record: first-party, flags and libnoise version unstated, no benchmark code, cellular gap likely algorithmic, cubic SSE2 slower than scalar FastNoise, archived and deprecated for FastNoise2.
